title: Electron-Deficient Cu Sites on Cu3Ag1 Catalyst Promoting CO2 Electroreduction to Alcohols
abstract: DOI: 10.1002/aenm.202001987 carbon sources through different technical routes,[1] which either have negative environmental impacts or deliver a poor atomic economy while being energy intensive.[2] For instance, the life-cycle greenhouse gas emission for producing a liter of bioethanol is ≈1.6 kg CO2 equivalent.[3] For fuel ethanol with a global production of ≈104 billion liters per year,[4] the annual CO2 emission is more than 170 million metric tons, corresponding to 0.5% of the global annual overall carbon emission.[5] New technologies are thus in demand to balance the target of environmental protection and economic development. Electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) driven by renewable energies is a competitive candidate, as it converts CO2 into liquid products like formate and alcohols with nearly net-zero CO2 emissions.[6] Nonetheless, the Faradaic efficiency (FE) for CO2-to-alcohol production generally remains low, typically less than 50%.[7] For instance, Gewirth and co-workers presented a nano porous Cu–Ag alloy for the enhancement of ECR activity, with an FE toward ethanol of ≈25%.[8] Bell and co-workers reported a Cu–Ag alloy with stain effect, and the total FE of alcohol production was less than 15%.[9] Recently, Sargent and co-workers reported an enhancement of ethanol selectivity in a flow cell system by tuning binding site diversity in an Ag/ Cu catalyst, while the FE for ethanol was still less than 50%.[10] The challenge in developing effective strategies of tuning the energetics of reaction pathways limits the CO2-to-alcohol selectivity. Based on the theoretical and experimental studies,[11] ethylene (C2H4) generally dominates the C2+ product distribution, with a theoretical prediction of an alcohol/ethylene ratio of 35:65.[12] However, Calle-Vallejo and Koper reported that ethanol presents a lower free energy position compared to ethylene in the entire reaction route of carbon monoxide (CO) electroreduction to C2 products.[13] The poor alcohol selectivity has been attributed to the unfavorable adsorption of key intermediates in the ethanol pathway on copper,[13] such as CH3CHO* and CH3CH2O* proved by Chorkendorff and co-workers.[14] Thus, it is rational to hypothesize that an enhanced alcohol selectivity may arise from modulating the adsorption of key intermediates like CH3CH2O* in the ECR pathways. In addition, it is also well known that Ag component can suppress hydrogen Copper-based catalysts electrochemically convert CO2 into multicarbon molecules. However, the selectivity toward alcohol products has remained relatively low, due to the lack of catalysts favoring the adsorption of key intermediates in the alcohol pathways. Herein, a Cu3Ag1 electrocatalyst is developed using galvanic replacement of an electrodeposited Cu matrix. The Cu3Ag1 electrocatalyst enables a 63% Faradaic efficiency for CO2-to-alcohol production and an alcohol partial current density of −25 mA cm−2 at −0.95 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode, corresponding to a 126-fold enhancement in selectivity and 25-fold increase in activity compared to the bare electrodeposited Cu matrix. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the interphase electron transfer from Cu to Ag generates electron-deficient Cu sites and favors the adsorption of CO2 reduction intermediates in the alcohol pathway, such as CH3CHO* and CH3CH2O*. Thus, for this electron-deficient catalyst, the C2H5OH pathway is more preferable than the ethylene (C2H4) pathway, endowing the catalyst with an alcohol/ethylene ratio of 38:1. These findings suggest both experimental approaches and theoretical insights for exploring highly selective CO2-to-alcohol conversion.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Alcohols, such as methanol, ethanol, and n-propanol, play essential roles in the modern chemical industry. To date, the manufacture of alcohols heavily relies on fossil and biomass
Adv. Energy Mater. 2020, 2001987
© 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH2001987 (2 of 8)
evolution reaction (HER), through which the ECR activity can be enhanced.[15]
In this work, we developed an adsorption tuning strategy via creating electronic deficiencies in Cu catalysts. A silver-doped copper matrix catalyst (designated as Cu3Ag1) was fabricated using a combination of Cu electrodeposition and subsequent galvanic replacement by Ag(I) (Figure  1a). Attributed to the interphase electron transfer from Cu to Ag, this Cu3Ag1 catalyst was identified as an electron-deficient structure to serve as the catalytic centers. Electrochemical experiments confirmed that this adsorption-tuned Cu3Ag1 catalyst exhibited a 63% total FE for alcohol production (mainly ethanol and n-propanol, Figure  1b), with a peak alcohol/ethylene ratio of 38:1. The alcohol selectivity was more than 90%, corresponding to a 126-fold enhancement in selectivity and 25-fold increase in activity compared to the originally electrodeposited Cu matrix without galvanic replacement. Furthermore, we investigated the mechanistic pathway using density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on a fully optimized slab model (Figure S1, Supporting Information), which revealed that the electrondeficient catalyst promotes the alcohol production via enhancing the adsorption of key alcohol-pathway intermediates, such as CH3CHO* and CH3CH2O*.

sections.heading: 2.1. Structural Characterizations
sections.text:
X-ray diffraction (XRD) of Cu3Ag1 and the Cu matrix (“Methods” in the Supporting Information) was first conducted to investigate the structural changes caused by introducing Ag, from which both samples displayed high crystallinities (Figure  2a). The intensity ratios between the Cu (200) and Cu (111) peaks
were 16.9, 2.87, and 2.69 for the Cu foil, Cu matrix, and Cu3Ag1, respectively, indicating that the electrodeposited Cu particles were (200)-oriented, although the orientation was relatively weaker than the original substrates (i.e., Cu foil), which was ascribed to the lower surface energy of Cu (111) plane in electrodeposition.[16] The average crystallite sizes were calculated as ≈36 and 65  nm for Cu matrix and Cu3Ag1 catalyst, respectively (Figure 2b). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images revealed the emergence of polyhedron particles (Figure S2, Supporting Information) after galvanic replacement, which was ascribed to the surface etching by chlorine ion.[17] High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy image (HAADF-STEM) also confirmed the dendritic morphology of the Cu3Ag1 catalyst (Figure S3a, Supporting Information). Energy dispersive X-ray spectra (EDS) indicated that silver was mainly distributed on the surface of copper matrix (Figure S3b–d, Supporting Information).
The atomic structures were then investigated by highresolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, Figure 2c) and STEM (Figure  2d). For the Cu matrix, Cu (200) and Cu (111) planes were observed, with the lattice constants calculated as ≈0.354  nm. For the Cu3Ag1 catalyst, similar orientations of Cu planes were also observed in both HRTEM (Figure 2e) and STEM (Figure 2f) images, while the calculated lattice constant was ≈0.364  nm. The slight increase in lattice constant was likely to be caused by the Ag dopants. In addition, dislocations (yellow circle in Figure  2e) and twin boundaries (blue circle in Figure  2e) were also observed upon the Ag doping. These results were consistent with the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) analyses (Figure S4, Supporting Information), which revealed the lattice constants of 0.354 and 0.364 nm, for Cu matrix and Cu3Ag1, respectively.
To gain insight into the electronic structures, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was further conducted to investigate

The surface Cu/Ag ratio was found to be 3:1, which was much lower than that of the bulk (Cu/Ag = 69:1) obtained using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) analysis. The results confirmed that Ag dopants were mainly distributed on the catalyst surface. The binding energy (B.E.) positions of Cu 2p3/2 shifted from 932.3 eV (in Cu matrix) to 932.7 eV (Cu3Ag1, the red arrows in Figure 3a). The same trends were confirmed for Cu 2p1/2 peaks, with the binding energies shifting from 952.0 eV (Cu matrix) to 952.6 eV (Cu3Ag1) (Figure 3a). This binding energy shift of Cu was attributed to the interphase electron transfer from Cu to Ag atoms, during which Cu atoms (i.e., electron donor) became electron deficient.[18] As the electron acceptor, the binding energy of Ag presented a reverse shifting (Figure  3b). The binding energies of Ag 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 peaks shifted from 374.3 and 368.4 eV (in Ag powder) to 374.2 and 368.2 eV (in Cu3Ag1), respectively.
To better understand the interaction between Cu and Ag, X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) were further conducted. The XANES spectra at Cu K-edge confirmed the edge features (assigned to 1s→4p transitions)[19] of electrodeposited Cu matrix and Cu3Ag1 samples, which were similar to those of commercial Cu foil reference (dot lines in Figure 3c, upper panel), indicating the existence of major copper phase. A similar phenomenon was observed for silver (Figure  3c, lower panel). The EXAFS spectra in k-space (Figure S5, Supporting Information) revealed a decrease of the Debye–Waller factor (i.e., increased disorder) after doping. The wavelet transform analysis[20] confirmed the difference between the Cu matrix and Cu3Ag1 samples (Figure 3d). The Cu–Cu region in Cu3Ag1 was located at ≈6.7 Å−1, exhibiting an apparent blueshift in the wavenumber compared to that of the Cu matrix (at ≈6.3 Å−1) or commercial Cu foil reference (centered at ≈6.6 Å−1), suggesting an increased CuCu bond length after the Ag doping. sections.heading: 2.2. Electrochemical Measurements
sections.text:
The electrochemical tests were conducted to assess the ECR performances of the electron-deficient Cu3Ag1 catalyst and Cu matrix. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) test was first conducted in an Ar-saturated 0.5 m KHCO3 electrolyte to investigate the Cu–Ag interaction. As shown in the CV curves (Figure  4a; Figure S7, Supporting Information), the Cu2+/Cu+ reduction peak shifted from 0.55 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE, for the Cu matrix, black curve) to 0.51 V versus RHE (for the Cu3Ag1, red curve), suggesting that the electron deficiency of surface Cu atoms in Cu3Ag1 led to more stable CuO and CuOH after etching.[21] The Ag+/Ag reduction peak (≈0.60 V vs RHE) was also observed for the Cu3Ag1 catalyst, suggesting the existence of surface Ag atoms (black arrows in Figure 4a).
The electrochemically active surface areas (ECSAs)[22] were evaluated by the Pb underpotential deposition (Pb-UPD) method.[23] The ECSAs of the Cu matrix and Cu3Ag1 were calculated as 2728 and 8876 cm2 gCu−1, respectively (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The ECSA increased after the Ag doping was ascribed to the enhanced randomness in crystal structure (e.g., more defects and interfaces) and strengthened porousness.[24] However, the Cu3Ag1 catalyst presented an ECSA-normalized alcohol partial current density (norJalcohol) of 2.31 mA cm−2 at −0.95 V versus RHE, nearly two orders of magnitude higher than that of the electrodeposited copper matrix (i.e., norJalcohol ≈ 0.007 mA cm−2 on bare Cu matrix). This result suggested that the high surface area was not the main contributor to the enhanced ethanol selectivity and activity of the Cu3Ag1 catalyst.
The ECR performances were then evaluated in CO2-saturated 0.5 m KHCO3 electrolyte. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of the Cu3Ag1 catalyst showed that the total current density reached 10 mA cm−2 at −0.40  V versus RHE (Figure  4b). A new peak was observed at ≈−0.90 V versus RHE (Figure 4b), attributed to the *CO adsorption on the Cu sites.[25] This new peak suggested the high coverage of *CO on the Cu surface after the formation of electron-deficient Cu sites in the Cu3Ag1 catalyst. In contrast, to reach the same current density of 10 mA cm−2, the Cu matrix and commercial Cu foil reference required −0.60 and −0.75 V versus RHE, respectively.
The FE and partial current density for each ECR product obtained were then measured and compared. For the Cu matrix, the H2 production was overwhelming on the electrode, with an FEH2 of ≈96% at −0.95 V versus RHE (Figure 4c, upper panel). In contrast, for the Cu3Ag1 catalyst, the FEH2 was inhibited to ≈27% at the same potential, while the overall FE for ethanol and n-propanol increased to 63% (Figure 4c, lower panel). Accordingly, the partial current densities for ethanol and n-propanol reached the maximum values of 17.2 and 7.3 mA cm−2 at −0.95  V versus RHE (Figure  4d). The total selectivity of alcohol among all ECR products (excluding H2) peaked at ≈92% at −0.95 V versus RHE (Figure 4e), suggesting a 126-fold enhancement in alcohol selectivity and a 25-fold increase in activity, compared to the electrodeposited Cu matrix (Figure 4f). Detailed nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and FE data were displayed (Figures S9 and S10, Supporting Information). Our data represented one of the best selectivities among the electrocatalysts reported for producing alcohols (Table S2,
Supporting Information). Moreover, an electrochemical reduction of CO was also conducted to identify the influence of CO produced on Ag. The alcohol selectivity on Cu matrix was only one quarter of that on Cu3Ag1 catalyst (Figure S11, Supporting Information) in CO atmosphere, suggesting that the CO-spillover mechanism[8,11] might not play an important role in our catalytic system.
The long-term ECR stability of the Cu3Ag1 catalyst was conducted at −0.95 V versus RHE for 18 h, which demonstrated a nearly constant total alcohol FE of 60 ± 3% (Figure 4g). The stability of the Cu3Ag1 electronic structure was investigated after the ECR operation. The deconvoluted XPS spectra presented similar spectra before and after the ECR test (Figure S12, Supporting Information). The EXAFS at the Ag K-edge confirmed a well-retained Ag–Cu interaction in samples collected after 15, 45, and 60 min of ECR test (dot line in Figure S6 of the Supporting Information). These results suggested that the electron-deficient Cu3Ag1 structure existed steadily during the experiments.

sections.heading: 2.3. Theoretical Calculations
sections.text:
To better understand the structure–effect correlation between the electronic structure of the Cu3Ag1 catalyst and alcohol selectivity, we studied the energetics of the CO2-to-alcohol pathway via DFT calculations. Given that the Cu3Ag1 and pure Cu matrix catalysts have an apparent Cu (100) orientation according to the XRD results (Figure 2a), Cu (100) surface having a Cu/Ag atomic ratio of 3:1, i.e., Cu3Ag1 (100), was built in our model. The calculation results revealed the stabilization of alcoholpathway intermediates like CH3CH2O* on electron-deficient Cu atoms compared to the pure Cu (100). Specifically, we calculated the adsorption energies (ΔE) and adsorption free energy (ΔG) of CO2 and *CO species on pure Cu (100), Ag (100), and Cu3Ag1 (100) surfaces (Table S3, Supporting Information). We found that the Cu sites in Cu3Ag1 (100), as the active sites for ECR, have a *CO binding energy of ≈−1.00 eV. In contrast, Ag atoms on Cu3Ag1 or pure Ag surface only adsorb *CO but not CO2, with binding energies of −0.47 or −0.41 eV, respectively.
The free adsorption energies of H* species (ΔGH*) on these surfaces were then calculated. On a pure Cu surface, the ΔGH* is −0.16  eV, suggesting HER is predominant and blocks the reaction sites for ECR (Figure S13a, Supporting Information). Doping Ag into Cu causes an electron transfer from Cu to Ag atoms of 0.08 e per Ag atom, according to Bader charge analyses. Consequently, the ΔGH* increases to 0.14 eV, which suppresses HER and provides more sites for ECR.
We further calculated the reaction pathway and energy levels of different ECR intermediates on the Cu3Ag1 (100) surface (Figure 5a; Figure S13b, Supporting Information). At 0 V versus standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) applied potential, the CO2 reduction proceeds through the carboxyl (*COOH) pathway to form *CO intermediates on the Cu sites. When a potential of −0.82  V versus SHE is applied, all the elementary steps are downhill toward *COH (Figure S13b, red lines, Supporting Information). *COH then associates with another *CO, and finally is converted into C2H5OH through the formation of key alcohol intermediates, i.e., CH3CHO* and CH3CH2O* (Figure  5a) at 0  V versus SHE. More importantly, we found the decrease in the adsorption free energy of CH3CHO* and CH3CH2O* intermediates; they are 0.11 and 0.41 eV more stable on Cu3Ag1 (100) surface compared to their opponents in ethylene pathway (Figure 5b,c), which is in contrast to the previous report on bare Cu (100).[13] This result
demonstrates a more favorable alcohol production on Cu3Ag1 (100) surface than Cu (100) and agrees with the selectivities obtained in our ECR experiments. The relationship between alcohol selectivity and electron-deficient copper sites in Cu3Ag1 was therefore verified by DFT calculations. Taken together, we concluded that the electron deficiency of Cu atoms after the Ag doping contributed to stabilizing the adsorption of the key alcohol intermediates and weakening the hydrogen binding, as a result of electrocloud-density change at 3d orbitals.[26]

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we have developed an electron-deficient Cu3Ag1 catalyst through interphase electron transfer strategy. The introduction of Ag into Cu facilitated electron transfer from Cu to Ag, which generated electron-deficient Cu sites in the Cu3Ag1 catalyst. DFT calculations confirmed that the electron-deficient Cu sites particularly favored the adsorption of key ECR intermediates in the alcohol pathway such as CH3CHO* and CH3CH2O*. This finding was verified by the electrocatalytic performance of CO2-to-alcohol using the Cu3Ag1 catalyst. Our work has revealed the electron-deficient state of Cu atoms in Cu3Ag1 catalysts with ECR-to-alcohol selectivity and activity, and suggested new opportunities for designing highly alcoholselective ECR catalysts.
